questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Consider the following chemical reactions performed at identical temperature and volume:
Experiment I: $\text{X(g)} \rightleftharpoons 2\text{Y(g)}$
Experiment II: $\text{X(g)} \rightleftharpoons \text{Z(g)}$
The partial pressure of the reactant and product are denoted, respectively, by $p_{reactant}$ and $p_{product}$ during the course of the reactions. Assuming ideal gas behaviour, the correct plot of $p_{reactant}$ versus $p_{product}$ for Experiments I and II is:
questions.solution:
Let the initial partial pressure of reactant $X$ be $P_0$.

For Experiment I, $X(g) \rightleftharpoons 2Y(g)$. If the partial pressure of $X$ decreases by $x$, then the partial pressure of product $Y$ increases by $2x$.

We have $p_{\text{reactant}} = P_0 - x$ and $p_{\text{product}} = 2x$, which gives $x = \dfrac{p_{\text{product}}}{2}$.

Substituting this into the first equation, we get $p_{\text{reactant}} = P_0 - \dfrac{1}{2}p_{\text{product}}$. This represents a straight line with a slope of $-1/2$ and an x-intercept of $2P_0$.

For Experiment II, $X(g) \rightleftharpoons Z(g)$. If the partial pressure of $X$ decreases by $y$, then the partial pressure of product $Z$ increases by $y$.

We have $p_{\text{reactant}} = P_0 - y$ and $p_{\text{product}} = y$.

Substituting $y$, we get $p_{\text{reactant}} = P_0 - p_{\text{product}}$. This represents a straight line with a slope of $-1$ and an x-intercept of $P_0$.

Both equations are linear, so the plots must be straight lines. The line for Experiment II has a steeper negative slope ($-1$) compared to Experiment I ($-1/2$) and intersects the x-axis at a smaller value ($P_0$ vs $2P_0$). This correctly corresponds to the graph shown in option (4).

questions.q:
Consider the following reversible exothermic reaction in an aqueous solution with the equilibrium constant $K_c$ defined in terms of molarity, at temperature $T$.
$2 \mathbf{X}(\mathrm{aq}) \rightleftharpoons \mathbf{Y}(\mathrm{aq})+2 \mathbf{Z}(\mathrm{aq})$

The reaction is started with the species $\mathbf{X}$ only. The correct statement about this reaction is
options: At equilibrium, if the reaction mixture is diluted with water at the same temperature to double the total volume, the value of $K_c$ will be halved after the new equilibrium is established.
If the temperature of the equilibrium reaction mixture is increased, the concentration of species $\mathbf{Z}$ will decrease.
If a small amount of $\mathbf{X}$ is added to the equilibrium reaction mixture, the value of $K_c$ will be reduced after the new equilibrium is established.

questions.q:
Consider the following reversible reaction at a particular temperature and pressure,
$\mathrm{N}_2(\mathrm{~g})+3 \mathrm{H}_2(\mathrm{~g}) \rightleftharpoons 2 \mathrm{NH}_3(\mathrm{~g})$
for which the equilibrium constants in terms of mole fraction $(x)$ and partial pressure $(p)$ are defined as $K_x=\frac{x_{\mathrm{NH}_3}^2}{x_{\mathrm{N}_2} x_{\mathrm{H}_2}^3}$ and $K_P=\frac{p_{\mathrm{NH}_3}^2}{p_{\mathrm{N}_2} p_{\mathrm{H}_2}^3}$, respectively. Let an equilibrium mixture contain 3 mol of $\mathrm{N}_2, 1 \mathrm{~mol}$ of $\mathrm{H}_2$ and 1 mol of $\mathrm{NH}_3\left(K_x=8.33\right)$. Now, keeping the temperature constant, if 5 mol of $\mathrm{N}_2$ are added to this mixture, the correct statement(s) is/are
options: The equilibrium will shift to the left producing more $\mathrm{N}_2$, if the $\mathrm{N}_2$ addition is at constant pressure.
The equilibrium will shift to the right producing more $\mathrm{NH}_3$, if the $\mathrm{N}_2$ addition is at constant pressure.
The equilibrium will shift to the left producing more $\mathrm{N}_2$, if the $\mathrm{N}_2$ addition is at constant volume.
The equilibrium will shift to the right producing more $\mathrm{NH}_3$, if the $\mathrm{N}_2$ addition is at constant volume.
